topic: RAG Maturation: From Catch-all to Specialist
text:
HOOK (0-5s)
[on-screen: RAG IS NOT A MAGIC BULLET]
Most engineers are still treating RAG like a magic bullet for every data problem.
A colleague told me the other day that RAG is dead.

SETUP (5-20s)
He was comparing how Cursor handles context versus Claude Code.
Cursor relies on permanent embeddings.
It's fast.
It also creates a lot of noise and gets expensive quickly.
Claude Code takes a different path with grep and glob.

BODY (20-75s)
[on-screen: EXACT MATCHES > APPROXIMATIONS]
Regex-based search finds exact matches instead of semantic guesses.
No tokens are wasted on things you'll never query.
Approximations can mislead an agent in a complex codebase.
RAG was born out of necessity to give LLMs better context.
The problem is it lacks direction.
New tools are finally filling the gaps where vector search is inefficient and costly.
Grep and glob are my go-to for code navigation now.
Keyword search gets handled by BM25.
Embeddings are reserved for what actually requires semantic understanding.
Large documentation needs embeddings.
Variable names in a source file don't.

CTA (last 10s)
[on-screen: CHOOSE THE RIGHT TOOL]
RAG isn't dead.
It's just finally being used as a specialized tool instead of a catch-all.
The only question that matters is what kind of data you're dealing with.
How are you drawing the line between tools and cognitive logic in your stack?

#AIEngineering #RAG #SoftwareArchitecture #LLMs
idea_source: RAGs are dead — that's what a colleague said the other day. It stuck with me because RAG is one of the pillars of data engineering. But he was right, in a specific context. He was explaining how Cursor works vs Claude Code: Cursor uses permanent embeddings so the agent always knows where everything is, updated constantly as new code is generated. Fast, efficient. But pricey and creates noise in the data. Claude Code, on the other hand, uses grep and glob — regex-based search to find exactly what's needed. No wasted tokens embedding things you never query. Exact matches, not approximations. Approximations can mislead. The deeper insight: RAGs were born out of necessity — to give LLMs better context. But they lack direction. New tools fill the gaps where RAGs are inefficient and costly. Today I use grep and glob for specific code navigation, BM25 for keyword search, and I only embed what actually needs semantic search — large documentation, not everything. The question engineers should ask: what kind of data are you dealing with? That determines the tool. RAG is not dead. It's just finally being used correctly.
